title: Exposure therapy for PTSD
description: Prolonged exposure is a trauma-focused therapy: over about ten weeks, people revisit the memory of the trauma in a safe setting and gradually face reminders they have been avoiding, so that the fear can fade. Studies scanned people before and after therapy, while recalling that a signal had become safe, and at rest. Brightness and lines show the change since before treatment: warmer or a pulsing line means more than before, violet or a dashed line means less than before.
caveat: The findings come from three studies by two groups, with 16 to 66 people with PTSD; one compared therapy with a waiting list. Two measured how areas work together at rest, which is not the same as activity, and one measured activity while recalling that a signal had become safe. The left frontoparietal "executive control" areas are drawn on the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which is an assumption. The sources read do not report how the brain differed before treatment, so the first part is drawn at rest. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before therapy. The comparison here starts from each person's own level, so the brain is drawn at rest.

phases.name: Ten weeks of exposure
phases.caption: About ten weekly sessions of revisiting the trauma memory and facing reminders. People were not scanned during this time.

citations.authors: Helpman L, Marin MF, Papini S, Zhu X, Sullivan GM, Schneier F, Neria M, et al.
citations.title: Neural changes in extinction recall following prolonged exposure treatment for PTSD: A longitudinal fMRI study.
citations.quote: The same procedures were repeated 10 weeks later, after PTSD patients had completed prolonged exposure treatment.

phases.name: Remembering safety
phases.caption: While recalling that a signal had become safe, the rostral anterior cingulate is less active than before therapy, and works more closely with the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the subgenual cingulate.

citations.authors: Helpman L, Marin MF, Papini S, Zhu X, Sullivan GM, Schneier F, Neria M, et al.
citations.title: Neural changes in extinction recall following prolonged exposure treatment for PTSD: A longitudinal fMRI study.
citations.quote: The same procedures were repeated 10 weeks later, after PTSD patients had completed prolonged exposure treatment.

phases.name: At rest
phases.caption: At rest, the amygdala works more closely with the orbitofrontal cortex and the insula, the hippocampus with the medial prefrontal cortex, and the amygdala less closely with left frontal "control" areas. Larger decreases in some of these links went with larger improvements.

order.rationale: These come from separate studies scanned at rest. They are shown after the task finding only to show one measurement at a time.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: In one study, the body's sweat response during recall did not change on average after therapy, though changes in it went with improvement. These are small studies and not everyone improved.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: The rostral anterior cingulate was less active while recalling that a signal had become safe, after prolonged exposure, in one study of 16 people with PTSD. It is drawn on the pregenual anterior cingulate.

citations.authors: Helpman L, Marin MF, Papini S, Zhu X, Sullivan GM, Schneier F, Neria M, et al.
citations.title: Neural changes in extinction recall following prolonged exposure treatment for PTSD: A longitudinal fMRI study.
citations.quote: PTSD patients exhibited pre- to post-treatment reduction in rostral anterior cingulate cortex (rACC) activation during extinction recall, and increase in functional coherence between the rACC and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC).

citations.authors: Fonzo GA, Goodkind MS, Oathes DJ, Zaiko YV, Harvey M, Peng KK, Weiss ME, et al.
citations.title: Amygdala and Insula Connectivity Changes Following Psychotherapy for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
citations.quote: The amygdala and insula displayed widespread patterns of primarily subregion-uniform intrinsic connectivity change, including increased connectivity between amygdala and insula; increased connectivity of both regions with the ventral prefrontal cortex, frontopolar, and sensory cortices; and decreased connectivity of both regions with left fronto-parietal nodes of the executive control network.

citations.title: Amygdala and Insula Connectivity Changes Following Psychotherapy for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
citations.quote: Individuals (N=66) with a primary PTSD diagnosis participated in a randomized clinical trial of prolonged exposure therapy (N=36) vs. treatment waiting list (N=30).

connections.explanation: The amygdala worked together less with left frontoparietal "executive control" areas at rest after therapy, in one trial; larger decreases in amygdala-frontal links went with larger improvements. Drawn to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which is an assumption.
